description: Robot model scouting + swap-in harness. Jake can't find an 'Artificial Analysis for robot models'. Nothing equivalent exists; closest are RoboArena (crowd-sourced real-world pairwise evals, DROID setup), VLABench/LIBERO/SimplerEnv (simulation leaderboards: pi0, pi0.5, GR00T N1, etc.) and per-paper real-robot results. Deliver: (1) a living comparison table in plans/ of open-weight manipulation models (MolmoAct2, FLUX 3 Action, pi0/pi0.5, GR00T, SmolVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, LingBot-VLA, RDT, etc.) covering license, size, VRAM, inference latency, SO-101 or LeRobot checkpoint availability, fine-tuning needed, and published zero-shot/real-world results with sources. (2) A harness so any model can be tried on a rented GPU against our SO-101 arms and our hand with one command: a common policy-server interface (camera frames + instruction in, actions out), a rental setup script for the cheapest suitable GPU, and a fixed small task suite with a scoring sheet, so we build our own mini-leaderboard. Respect the human-mirror setup: two stereo cameras at eye height.

results.identified_issue: Model facts come from a web research pass dated 2026-10-16; where a source was unclear the table says '?' or 'unverified'. Deliberately deleted a separate transformers MolmoAct2 adapter: LeRobot now ships policy.type=molmoact2 and lerobot/MolmoAct2-SO100_101-LeRobot with the joint sign/offset fix built in, so one lerobot adapter covers every listed checkpoint. Unverified on first launch: RunPod REST fields dockerEntrypoint/dockerStartCmd/portMappings, the pip extras in models.json (molmoact2/flux3 need LeRobot from git), the smolvla_base/pi05_base image feature keys (the adapter raises at load if a policy view has no camera_map entry), and MolmoAct2 units (marked degrees from its sample state). The client's max-jump guard (default 25) is the backstop for unit/convention errors. Stdlib HTTP rather than LeRobot's gRPC async_inference: it serves non-LeRobot models too, enforces the two-eye contract and is testable without torch. Rejected: Vast (cheaper by cents but volatile, unverified hosts) and HF Jobs ($0.80/h L4); both noted in the plan.
results.summary: No real 'Artificial Analysis for robots' exists, so I wrote a sourced comparison table of 12 open models and built robot_eval/: one command rents a GPU, serves any model, runs a scored trial on our SO-101 with the two head cameras, and ranks results.
results.detailed_description:
Short answer: nothing like Artificial Analysis exists for robot models. The closest is Ai2's vla-evaluation-harness leaderboard, which collects self-reported simulation scores, and NVIDIA's RoboLab-120 (Franka, simulated). RoboArena is real-world but uses DROID setups. None of them reports results for an SO-101 with only head-height cameras, so the leaderboard that matters is one we score ourselves.

(1) plans/robot_model_scouting.md is a living table of 12 models: MolmoAct2, FLUX 3 Action, pi0.5, pi0/pi0-FAST, GR00T N1.7, SmolVLA, X-VLA, OpenVLA-OFT, LingBot-VLA v2, RDT2, Cosmos3-Nano and DreamZero. It covers license, size, VRAM, latency, SO-101/LeRobot checkpoint, expected cameras, zero-shot or fine-tune, and published results. Every number has a link; '?' means it isn't published. Takeaway: MolmoAct2 is the only one with an SO-101 checkpoint, a permissive license and two third-person camera views (close to our eye-height pair), so it stays the first zero-shot trial. FLUX 3 Action is strong, but its license forbids commercial robotics use and it expects a wrist camera. Everything else needs our own demos; SmolVLA (450M) is the cheapest to fine-tune.

(2) robot_eval/ is the harness. protocol.py is a single contract: instruction, joint state and exactly two JPEGs (left/right eye) in, an action chunk out; a wrist camera is rejected by design. server.py runs on the GPU and loads any LeRobot policy from a row in models.json (MolmoAct2, FLUX3, SmolVLA, pi0.5 and a mock), with a camera_map saying which eye feeds which model view. rent.py picks the cheapest RunPod Community GPU that fits: RTX 4090 at $0.34/h or A6000 48 GB at $0.33/h, as seen today. It starts the server and has up/status/down; down deletes the pod, because a stopped pod still bills. try.sh is the one command, e.g. 'bash robot_eval/try.sh molmoact2_so101 pick_block 1 --stereo-device 0'. It dry-runs unless you add --execute, asks you to score against the rubric, then deletes the GPU unless you say keep. tasks.json is six frozen tasks (touch, pick, block-in-bowl, colour choice, slide paper, pick paper), each with 5 trials on marked mat spots and a 3-point rubric. leaderboard.py turns scores.csv into a ranking, kept separate per end effector so the stock jaw and Hand 1.0 don't mix.

Safety, plus what's hardcoded: rows that are late, out-of-order, stale or non-finite are refused, and so is any chunk whose first move is far from the current pose (that catches unit or joint-sign mismatches). Every move is rate-limited, and a lost camera frame stops the trial instead of reusing an old one. The GPU list and prices are hardcoded in rent.py and will drift.

Verified: 18 stdlib tests pass, including a real HTTP round trip with the mock model and every rejection path. Not yet run: a real pod, real model loading, cameras or the arm. To go further I need a RunPod API key exported as RUNPOD_API_KEY with about $10 credit, plus HF_TOKEN with FLUX 3 / PaliGemma access accepted.
results.user_reply_draft: Hey — good question, and the honest answer is that nothing like Artificial Analysis exists for robot models yet. The closest boards test in simulation or on other people's robots, and none of them use our arm with head-height cameras. So we built two things: a comparison of the twelve open models worth looking at (license, size, GPU needs, speed, whether they work on the SO-101 out of the box, and published results with links), and a one-command way to rent a cheap GPU, run any of them on our arm and hand, and score it on the same six small tasks every time. That gives us our own leaderboard. MolmoAct2 is the one to try first. The next step is plugging in a GPU account and running the first real trials.

user_request.name: Is there such a thing as Artificial Analysis for robot models? There's a lot of robot models out there and I can't find what I'm looking for. I want to be able to try different ones on rented GPUs and run them with our hand or our SO-101 arms.

summary: No "Artificial Analysis for robot models" exists, so we need a living plans/ table comparing open-weight manipulation models (license, size, VRAM, latency, SO-101/LeRobot checkpoints, published results) plus a harness to test them. The harness needs a common policy-server interface, a cheapest-GPU rental script, and a fixed task suite with scoring sheet for SO-101 arms and our hand, using the two eye-height stereo cameras.
